sourceBindings.text: An old maize leaf falls onto the soil. How could some of its nitrogen eventually reach a new maize root? Follow the nutrient through a living soil, then distinguish that journey from movement between leaves inside the plant.
Explain mass flow, diffusion and root interception, identify the direction of each on an accurate root diagram, and give a qualified example for each.
Distinguish movement toward the root in soil from redistribution within the plant, and explain why mobile N, P and K deficiencies often appear first on older leaves.
Predict how water, root growth, soil structure or pH can affect availability without treating all nutrients as moving by the same route or roots as swallowing soil.

sourceBindings.text: Old maize leaves are returned to the field. A new maize plant begins to grow after the residues start decomposing.
Microbes break down some organic material and may mineralize N; other microbes may temporarily immobilize it.
Usable N ions, including nitrate, can enter soil water. Water movement can carry nitrate toward roots by mass flow.
The root absorbs suitable ions from the solution; neither the whole leaf nor soil particles are swallowed.
Nutrient cycling, travel to the root and membrane uptake are related but different stages.

sourceBindings.text: Phosphate concentration is lower immediately beside an active root than farther away in moist soil.
Identify the concentration gradient from the higher concentration farther out to the lower concentration at the root.
Draw the net diffusion arrow toward the root through connected soil water. Explain that dry or disconnected water films slow the process.
Diffusion follows a gradient and is not a claim that all phosphate in the soil is immediately available.

sourceBindings.text: A soil report detects nutrients, but the topsoil is dry and compacted and roots are short.
Limited water can reduce mass flow and diffusion, while compaction restricts root extension and interception.
Check roots, soil moisture, pH, crop stage and the test's available-nutrient interpretation before choosing a treatment.
Do not recommend more fertilizer only because the crop looks weak.
Presence, supply to the root and uptake are separate questions.

sourceBindings.text: On a blank root-in-soil cross-section, place three numbered arrow groups: (1) water plus dissolved ions toward the root for mass flow; (2) dissolved ions from higher to lower concentration toward the root for diffusion; (3) a root tip extending outward toward a nutrient-containing zone for interception. Add one sentence explaining why a root does not swallow soil.
This diagram practice does not diagnose a field or certify fertilizer treatment. Explain your reasoning as well as choosing arrows.

sourceBindings.text: Nutrient transport to roots and within plants
Question
Soil-to-root transport
Within-plant redistribution
Where?
Through soil water or growing root contact to the root surface
Between older and newer tissues after uptake
Main mechanisms taught here
Mass flow, diffusion and root interception
Remobilization of N, P and K from older tissue when supply is limiting
Diagnostic use
Explains why supply can fail despite nutrient presence
Helps decide which leaves to inspect first; does not prove the cause

sourceBindings.text: mass flow
Transport of dissolved nutrient ions with water moving through soil toward roots.
diffusion
Net movement of dissolved ions down a concentration gradient, for example toward a depleted root surface.
root interception
Contact with new soil regions as a root grows; it does not mean swallowing soil.
mineralization
Microbial conversion of organic-bound nutrient into mineral forms that may become plant-available.
internal remobilization
Movement of a nutrient from older plant tissues toward newer tissues when supply is limiting.

sourceBindings.text: Learner labels all three routes and their directions on a root cross-section; explains water-carried mass flow, concentration-driven diffusion and growth-driven root interception with nitrate, P/K and new root contact as qualified examples.
Pass only when all three mechanisms and arrows are correct and no route is claimed universal; otherwise targeted review and open retry.

Learner identifies soil-to-root transport and within-plant remobilization as different processes; explains older-leaf tendency for mobile N/P/K and contrasts, cautiously, with newer-growth symptoms of poorly mobile nutrients.
Pass when both locations and the reason for the older-leaf pattern are correct, without making leaf position a stand-alone diagnosis.
Given a dry or compacted soil, damaged root, or unsuitable pH, learner explains the plausible effect on nutrient supply and states what evidence is still needed.
Pass when the mechanism and uncertainty are justified; recommending fertilizer solely from a visible sign or a generic pH number does not pass.
